articles.title: US pressure needs to be directed at Russia, not Ukraine
articles.summary: Author David J. Kramer argues that the Trump administration must consistently defend American corporate interests and global market stability by increasing pressure on Russia to end its aggression against Ukraine.
articles.body:
As Russia escalates its deadly strikes against Ukraine and its civilian population, Ukraine is retaliating with strikes against Russian military and energy targets. The U.S. must be clear where it stands — with Ukraine and against Russia, the aggressor.

The Trump administration should also condemn assaults on American business operations in the region. Vice President JD Vance cautioned Ukraine on this, but he should make sure that Russia, too, knows America will not tolerate such actions.

Russia has struck American companies’ facilities in Ukraine dozens of times over the last year, including facilities belonging to Coca-Cola, Boeing, Mondelez, Cargill, and Philip Morris, among others. The administration has been silent in these cases. The White House, “despite its pledge to defend U.S. commercial interests abroad, has been muted in its response” to Russia’s attacks on U.S. interests in Ukraine, as the New York Times put it .

When Ukraine struck the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal in the Russian port of Novorossiysk in the Black Sea, Vance called Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky July 31 to express concern that Ukraine was “destabilizing oil markets and harming U.S. companies by targeting tankers carrying crude” piped from Kazakhstan to the terminal, in which Chevron and ExxonMobil own stakes.

American leaders’ intervention when U.S. companies come under attack is appropriate. But leaders should be consistent in defending American corporate interests by applying pressure on Moscow, not just on Ukraine. After all, Russia is the true aggressor in this war. In fact, since Russia invaded Ukraine for no good reason, the administration should be pressuring Moscow even more than Ukraine.

Russia President Vladimir Putin should be held accountable for the deaths of and injuries to hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians, as well as for the hundreds of billions of dollars in damage to Ukraine’s economy. He also bears responsibility for some 1.5 million Russians killed and wounded needlessly. Ukrainian strikes against Russian targets represent retaliation for a war Putin started but refuses to end, while also degrading his military capabilities.

Ukraine has inflicted serious damage on Russian military and energy facilities. It has recently hit Russia’s equivalent of Amazon, called “Wildberries,” in places all over Russia. Ukrainian officials claim Wildberries provides support for the Russian military , but their strikes are also giving Russians a taste of what Ukrainians have been enduring for a long time.

Ukraine has every right to defend itself, and going after Russian energy sources is a way of depriving Moscow of the energy revenue that sustains its military aggression.

In addition to hitting American corporate interests in Ukraine, Russia has been deliberately targeting Ukrainian ports in Odesa, from which Ukraine exports significant amounts of agricultural goods, fertilizer and other products. If the administration is concerned about turmoil on the global markets, it should press Russia to halt such attacks.

Before Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Mark Temnycky notes in Forbes , Ukraine “ranked seventh among global producers for wheat production, sixth for corn production, fourth for barley production, and second for sunflower oil,” according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data . When Russia disabled Ukrainian Black Sea ports in 2022, the disruption to trade then helped drive global food prices to record highs .

Russian attacks on Ukrainian facilities in Odesa amid the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz will now add further stress to global markets. The Trump administration should be pressing the Russians to stop these attacks.

U.S. pressure on Moscow shouldn’t be limited to Russian strikes in the Black Sea, of course. The U.S., together with our European and other allies, should be doing everything to apply pressure on Putin to stop his aggression and pull back his troops that are occupying Ukrainian territory. This is best done by providing serious and rapid military assistance to Ukraine and tightening sanctions on Russia, with the goal of helping Ukraine win and defeat Russia, so that Putin doesn’t attack again.

Thanks to CIA Director John Ratcliffe, the U.S. continues providing critical intelligence to Ukraine . The Ukrainians return the favor by providing the American side vital insights into Russia’s capabilities on the battlefield.

Earlier this year, Vance claimed that ending U.S. military assistance to Ukraine is “one of the things I’m proudest that we’ve done in this administration.” In light of that, it is surprising that the Ukrainians listened to his recent request. But since the Ukrainian government is in desperate need of interceptor missiles to thwart constant Russian ballistic missile attacks and continued intelligence-sharing, it needs to avoid alienating the U.S. administration, even if both the current and previous administrations have disappointed Kyiv numerous times.

By helping Ukraine and pressuring Russia, the Trump administration can expedite an end to the war. That, in turn, would protect American companies in the region, help stabilize global markets, and save innocent Ukrainian lives.

David J. Kramer is executive director of the George W. Bush Institute and a former deputy assistant secretary of state for Europe and Eurasia during the George W. Bush administration.

articles.title: Service resumes on CrossCountry trains after power outage
articles.summary: It follows major national rail disruption at the weekend.
articles.body:
Train operator CrossCountry says it expects to run a full service on Monday after cancelling nearly all of its UK services the day before following a power cut at its control centre.

The outage in Birmingham at the weekend brought disruption from Glasgow to Penzance.

Major routes were affected between Birmingham and Manchester, which pass through Stoke-on-Trent, Coventry and Wolverhampton. Journeys from Leeds to York and Cheltenham to Cardiff were also caught in the travel chaos, leaving passengers frustrated.

On Monday morning, CrossCountry reported a handful of service cancellations, although these were put down to trains departing late and staff shortages.

Customers are advised to check their journey before travelling.

The operator on Sunday thanked passengers for their patience and understanding during the disruption.

Tickets purchased for travel on CrossCountry services on Sunday will be valid for travel on CrossCountry services until Wednesday, the company has said.

On Sunday, a range of personal experiences were shared by passengers.

Andy Burton, from Worcester, was travelling back from Cromford to Worcester after spending the weekend away with family celebrating his sister's birthday, but only got as far as Derby before his journey came to a premature end.

He was forced to stay the night in a budget hotel in the hope he could return home on Monday.

"It was only once I had arrived at Derby that a member of staff told me my planned alternative route via Leicester had also been cancelled, because it was part of the CrossCountry disruption," he said.

"I soon realised I was stranded, as they said there was no alternative train route back to Worcester.

"It's not the best end to a great weekend away."

Reese Proctor described the cancellations as "frustrating and unacceptable" as he tried to get to Manchester's Etihad Stadium in time for a 14:00 BST kick-off against Bournemouth.

He had hoped to get a train from Reading to Manchester, but instead resorted to driving more than 100 miles to his friend's house in Leicester before driving on to the stadium.

The 22-year-old told BBC Newsbeat the drive had added an extra two hours to his journey, leaving him "fuming".

A number of services resumed on Sunday evening, including an hourly train service from Birmingham New Street to Leicester and Derby.

On Sunday, Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said she was "concerned" by the situation.

She said: "We are setting up Great British Railways and nationalising services, including CrossCountry next year, to end decades of fragmentation and vulnerability on our network. We are determined to give passengers the reliability they deserve."

The National Union of Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers (RMT) has called for a review of railway operational control centres following the disruption, "to ensure they remain unaffected by power outages".

RMT general secretary Eddie Dempsey said passengers and rail workers should not have to face another week of "travel chaos" because of unreliable back-up systems.

CrossCountry was ranked Britain's worst rail operator in June.

articles.title: Guinea rubbish landfill collapse kills 31 in Conakry
articles.summary: A mound of rubbish at a major waste site buried several homes in the capital, the government says.
articles.body:
At least 31 people have been killed after a mound of rubbish at a major waste site collapsed onto nearby homes in Guinea's capital Conakry, the government has said.

Another 22 people were injured, including six seriously, in the city's Dar-es-Salam area.

"Significant" resources and personnel - including the military - were deployed to search for survivors after the collapse at about 02:00 local time following heavy rain overnight, the government added in a statement.

One woman told local media her five children had died in the disaster. There are fears that the death toll will rise further.

Rescuers were later seen using excavators to comb through a mountain of scattered rubbish at the site as local residents gathered nearby.

One eyewitness said many people were buried when a second part of the site gave way.

"People tried to come to the rescue [after the first section collapsed]... They came running and climbed onto the refuse to see if anyone was there," Robert Kamano Sâa told the Associated Press.

"That was when the second section collapsed in three successive stages, cascading down. And that is what poured onto the people."

Guinea's Prime Minister Mamadou Oury Bah has visited the scene to assess the situation and oversee the search efforts.

Mamadouba Bangoura, who lost his house in the collapse, said he and his family were woken up by the "loud noise" of the first wave of rubbish, which did not reach them.

"[Then] the second wave came. That is what knocked over - pushed the house - and it fell," he told Reuters news agency.

"There were a lot of people [buried]... It is very, very difficult to talk about it because seeing a human being lose their life like that is pathetic, it is so painful."

Neighbourhood leader Lancine Sylla had earlier told the AFP news agency that he feared there would be a heavy death toll.

"We have pulled out 18 bodies that were taken to the morgue," he said.

Visiting the injured in hospital, Health Minister Khaïté Sall said they would get free medical care, while assuring families of government support.

Guinea has experienced similar landslide tragedies before, with 10 people being killed at the same site in 2017.

The government had recently ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay.

Guinea's opposition figure and former Prime Minister Cellou Dalein Diallo, who is in exile abroad, called the accident "a tragedy that plunges us into dismay".

"This tragedy is all the more worrying because the closure of the landfill had been announced for this Sunday, 23 August", he said.

Rescue teams are continuing to search through the waste for others trapped underneath.

Go to BBCAfrica.com for more news from the African continent.

articles.title: Viral Cat in the Hat TikTok trend sparks fake videos and real fear
articles.summary: The social media posts have prompted police forces in Ireland and the UK to issue statements that the images are fake.
articles.body:
"He's so scary!" says 16-year-old Skye, recoiling at the mention of the Cat in the Hat.

Viral images purporting to show a life-sized version of the Dr Seuss character on the streets after dark have sparked fear and confusion among teenagers.

The posts, seen by millions, have convinced some young people that the character is real and that they might encounter it, prompting police forces in Ireland and the UK to issue statements confirming that the images and videos are fake.

"I was having a sleepover," Skye elaborates, "but everyone started watching Cat in the Hat videos. It was 3am. I wanted to go home. When I started walking down my friends' driveway, I got totally freaked out that the Cat in the Hat was going to jump out. I had to call my mum to pick me up."

A quick scroll through TikTok reveals numerous accounts, many of them created in the past few weeks, sharing photos and videos of an elusive black-and-white feline wearing the famous, towering, crooked red-and-white striped hat.

One post showing the original Cat in the Hat costume, accompanied by the caption "Help, what do I do?", has received 14.6m views in just three weeks.

The comments add to the sense of frenzy, with followers asking, "Why is he taxidermied?" Others zoom in on parts of the costume and post conspiracy theories about Mike Myers, who played the character in the 2003 film, being trapped inside.

Another popular account set up this week, posts videos of a real person dressed in a cat in the hat costume, dancing, with captions like "Kent I'm coming. lock your doors." Other users are sharing the videos, adding their own captions and locations across the UK.

Many of the AI generated images have been centred on the Irish counties of Limerick and Wexford, where shaky videos purportedly showed the character wandering through the streets, causing alarm and confusion among residents.

In Wexford, the local Gardaí (police force) quickly dismissed the sightings as fake and confirmed that the images had been generated using artificial intelligence.

That has not stopped the pictures and videos from spreading online - along with unverified claims posted without evidence that the Cat in the Hat has been involved in violent assaults.

"I low-key wanna go meet him…" says 14-year-old Lily, who heard that the Cat in the Hat had arranged a "meet and greet", inviting local TikTok followers to come to the woods in Galashiels, a small town in the Scottish Borders.

Her mother was horrified by the prospect.

"You are not going to meet anyone in the woods in the middle of the night!" she told her.

There is a point at which viral dancing videos and AI-generated clips of the Cat in the Hat become something potentially more sinister, with real-world consequences beyond their impact on teenage imaginations.

In England, South Yorkshire Police has denied social media claims that a 'killer Cat in the Hat' has been spotted. Posts about the alleged sightings have attracted hundreds of thousands of views on TikTok.

There is also a fake Facebook post also claiming to be from South Yorkshire Police - and suggesting that the force is taking the rumoured sighting seriously.

In response, a South Yorkshire Police spokesperson said: "If you do see posts online providing policing updates and advice, please check that they are from an official policing account. The cat is not out of the hat on this one… Please don't believe everything you read on social media."

As with so many trends driven by TikTok, comedic reaction and spoofery is what will be appearing right now on many people's For You page.

In recent days, depending largely on what your algorithm serves up, you may be seeing nearly as many people in Cat in the Hat costumes dancing to Beyonce as those stalking the streets. There are several jokey videos depicting police chasing human sized cats, and Scottish drag performer Ellie Diamond has issued a video declaring that she is not the Cat in the Hat killer.

And Irish TikTok star Garron Noone said on one post that it should have been obvious it was a hoax "because even the most soulless, evil, vicious monster" would be "traumatised looking in the window of a Wexford person".

Snapchat filters and images shared in group chats suggest that many teenagers - and those not so young - are simply having harmless fun with the trend.

But some do remain perturbed, including another teenager in the Scottish borders, 16-year-old Ellie, who says: "I was so scared of him when I was little," Ellie confides. "Now it's like he's actually come to life to haunt me."

A post on X that appears to have accelerated the current viral phenomenon appears to have been made on 8 August, by DiscussingFilm, when the pop culture site posted that the original costume was being auctioned off by Propstore.

The post has 10 million views. Comments describe it as "nightmare fuel" and "genuinely haunting", suggesting it had been pulled from a 'cursed attic'.

The lot is scheduled to be sold on Wednesday as part of an auction of 1,400 pieces of film and TV memorabilia and is predicted to fetch a price of up to $24,000 (£17,500).

Emily, a mother in Scotland, says the trend reminds her of the "Momo Challenge", a notorious internet hoax and digital urban legend. At the time, fact-checkers and authorities found no verified evidence linking the meme to children harming themselves, although the frightening images were still capable of causing distress.

"I'm not worried about my daughters, but there could be people with bad intentions who might take advantage of this trend to manipulate teenagers."

For now, the evidence points not to a real, roaming Cat in the Hat, but to a rapidly evolving online story built from an auctioned film costume, people in costume, AI-generated material and unverified posts.

Whether the claims began as a joke or were deliberately designed to frighten and manipulate, the advice from police is the same: pause before sharing, check the original source and date, look for confirmation from official police accounts, and treat invitations to meet strangers, especially at night or in isolated places, as a serious warning sign.

The rapidly evolving trend terrorising or tantalising teenagers on TikTok across the UK and Ireland is a reminder that online fear can quickly spill into the real world.

articles.title: Pence denies that Iran war hurting Ukraine by depleting US stockpiles
articles.summary: Former Vice President Mike Pence denied Sunday that the U.S. military depleting its weapons stockpiles in the Iran war is hurting Ukraine in its ongoing fight against Russia. “I don’t see it that way, and I don’t think… the Ukrainians do either,” Pence told host Dana Bash on CNN’s “State of the Union,” while in…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Mike Pence denied Sunday that the U.S. military depleting its weapons stockpiles in the Iran war is hurting Ukraine in its ongoing fight against Russia.

“I don’t see it that way, and I don’t think… the Ukrainians do either,” Pence told host Dana Bash on CNN’s “State of the Union,” while in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv.

“As I talked to President Zelensky, he made it very clear that they have the ability to deal with the drone warfare,” Pence added.

The former vice president addressed the National Prayer Breakfast in Ukraine on Sunday and spoke with Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky.

The U.S. military has exhausted nearly 80 percent of its terminal high-altitude area defense missile interceptors since the start of the Iran war, CNN reported earlier this month .

The Pentagon has also burned through roughly half of its Patriot interceptors since the conflict began, according to CNN.

Analysts from the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated in May it would take the U.S. until mid-2029 to replenish its Patriot stockpiles to their prewar inventory.

That depletion comes as Russian forces continue to strike Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv. July saw the highest monthly total of Ukrainian civilian casualties in the war since March 2022, the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission reported earlier this month .

“Civilians are facing intensified risks from the increased use of missiles and drones in urban centers, glide bombs in cities closer to the frontline, and short-range drones,” said Danielle Bell, the head of the mission’s Ukraine office.

“Together, these attacks are driving up civilian casualties across different regions of Ukraine,” Bell noted.

Pence referenced the increases in Russian strikes, saying Russian President Vladimir Putin has authorized the use of high-arc ballistic missiles “in an act of desperation.”

The former vice president also said Zelensky told him he expects Russian forces to strike energy infrastructure sites in Ukraine as the winter grows closer. To combat that, Pence said Zelensky requested 5 percent of the U.S. military’s remaining Patriot inventory.

“He said, ‘We’re looking just for 5 percent of your remaining Patriot inventory,’ and he believes that would get them through the winter months,” Pence told Bash.

“If we give them what they need, they’re going to secure their sovereignty and a peaceful and just future,” the former vice president later remarked, referring to Ukraine. “I just know it with all my heart.”

articles.title: Carney says US ‘attacked’ Canada with tariffs
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sunday said the U.S. attacked Ottawa with tariffs, escalating a trade war that will impact residents on both sides of the border. “In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits for Canada and called into question the reliability of…
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sunday said the U.S. attacked Ottawa with tariffs, escalating a trade war that will impact residents on both sides of the border.

“In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits for Canada and called into question the reliability of any deal,” Carney said during a press conference on Sunday in response to a question from a journalist who asked why it felt like the nation was going to war.

“In short, they asked too much and they offered too little. You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked,” he added in reference to the Trump administration’s tariffs.

The 50 percent U.S. tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods went into effect early Sunday morning and were authorized under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930.

The new levies bypass prior exemptions for goods under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), which is a free trade pact that entered into force on July 1, 2020, replacing the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).

The U.S. declined to sign a 16-year renewal of the agreement during the 2026 review period, unless concessions were made by both Canada and Mexico.

New tariffs introduced by President Trump apply duties to products like dairy, wine and furniture.

This direct override of traditional protections — combined with stalled negotiations and a looming Canadian dollar-for-dollar retaliation — places the future of the USMCA in serious doubt.

Carney has a background in economics and previously served as governor of both the Bank of Canada and the Bank of England before becoming prime minister.

He’s refused to play passive with the White House and on Friday said Ottawa would retaliate as a result of the heightened tariffs.

“We have recognized from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship,” Carney said.

“Canada has what the world wants. And we will not allow any nation to determine our future.”

Meanwhile, Trump has accused Canada of requesting benefits that would only be granted to a U.S. state not a foreign country or trade partner.

“Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!! They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!” the president wrote in an early Sunday morning Truth Social post .

articles.title: Yr Wyddfa rows between people queuing and those skipping the line
articles.summary: There has been disagreement between queuers and others skipping the line to reach the top of Yr Wyddfa.
articles.body:
Visitors to Wales' highest mountain are being urged to respect others by not skipping queues to reach the top following rows among climbers.

Recent hot weather means there have been bumper summer crowds at Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, where people have reportedly waited more than one hour to reach the 1,085m (3,560ft)-high summit.

Social media videos have shown arguments among queue-jumpers and those patiently waiting their turn to touch the metal plate that marks the top.

A recent video showed Marc Screeton, from Manchester, being heckled as he bypassed the line, saying: "Imagine queuing on a mountain? No chance."

But others have said queuing is necessary for safety reasons.

Eryri National Park Authority said its policy remained one of "self-policing" at the summit.

The mountain's growing popularity in Eryri National Park, also known as Snowdonia, has led to bottlenecks, and queues are now common on the stone steps leading to a metal plate or trig point where people pose for photos and videos.

Two charity hikers raising money for motor neurone disease were booed after skipping queues to reach the summit in May.

Speaking to BBC Wales, walkers on the mountain had mixed views about those jumping the queues.

Lucy Taylor said: "I think you should queue because it's really quite dangerous and everyone's trying to get up there - it's just not safe."

Tina Millard from West Bromwich said: "I don't think that you should have to queue.

"It's a mountain, you should just be able to go up and that's it.

"We're not at Alton Towers for a ride. It's a mountain, it's for everyone," she said.

Carl Lynch from Dunstable, Bedfordshire said: "It should be: 'go up there, two minutes and then move on for everyone else'. Simple as that."

Throughout this year's hot weather national park wardens have urged visitors to follow the country code by leaving gates as they found them, taking their litter away with them and reducing the risks of wildfires.

They have also urged people to wait their turn when queuing.

Alun Jones, an area warden for Eryri National Park Authority, urged those wanting to reach the trig point to be "considerate and don't skip the queue".

While queuing is often not compulsory, it is often an "unwritten and unspoken" social contract, according to an expert in moral philosophy.

Johann Go, who is also assistant professor of ethics at University College London, said: "So it's not that I have to queue, but given that others are already restraining themselves, if I were to then jump the queue, I would be saying 'to hell with them' and that my time is more valuable."

In May a pair of charity hikers were met with jeers from a queue at the summit as they tapped the trig point to complete a charity challenge.

Jamie Richardson, 32, and Richard Thiedeman, 34, from Lincolnshire, were climbing Yr Wyddfa as part of the Three Peaks challenge to raise money for their friend who has motor neurone disease (MND).

"I was getting booed and then there was a gentleman who was at the top, who had just had his photo taken and he physically tried to stop me," Richardson said.

He said he had just touched the summit point and heard someone say "you should be ashamed of yourself".

Richardson added: "There's no policing of it at all, it is purely free will, if you want to queue you can.

"The queuing, that is just purely down to British culture traditions."

On social media, some described the scenes at the mountain over the May bank holiday weekend as having a carnival atmosphere due to the crowds there.

A spokesman for the Eryri National Park Authority said it had "no plans to intervene in a dispute over hikers queuing at the top of Yr Wyddfa".

He said: "There are three quarters of a million people summitting annually, so queues are likely to be expected in peak times."

He added there were no plans for new measures to be implemented this year, but the matter would be discussed at an end of visitor season meeting in the early autumn.

articles.title: Massive garbage heap collapses onto homes, killing at least 30 as rescuers search for survivors
articles.summary: A mountain of garbage collapsed after heavy rain at a major landfill site in Conakry, Guinea, burying nearby homes and launching a search for survivors.
articles.body: At least 30 people were killed in a massive landslide in Guinea on Sunday when a mountainous open-air landfill collapsed and buried nearby shacks, trapping numerous victims beneath a mass of garbage. The incident happened at Dar Es Salam, the largest waste dump in the West African country's capital, Conakry, according to a report from The Associated Press (AP). Guinea News reported that the weight of the waste caused a three-story building beneath it to cave in. Authorities said heavy rainfall also washed over the refuse overnight, creating hazardous conditions at the landfill, according to The AP. EARTHQUAKE SHAKES PERU'S ANDES REGION, KILLING AT LEAST 5, DISPLACING HUNDREDS Six people were seriously injured and several homes were destroyed in the incident, according to reports. Officials launched a search-and-rescue operation to find any survivors. The AP reported that the landfill was originally scheduled to close Sunday after officials warned of hazardous conditions, citing Lt. Col. Baldé Mamadou Bailo, the sanitation officer for the military engineering battalion. The decision followed reports of a similar incident at the landfill in recent years, raising concerns about its safety. As a precautionary measure, residents who lived near the site had also been given eviction notices and were forced to vacate the area, The AP said. However, many people remained nearby at the time of the disaster, according to reports. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We will ensure that the remaining families are relocated elsewhere," Dienabou Touré, the minister of territorial administration and decentralization, said at the scene, according to The AP. Reuters reported that the landfill suffered a similar incident in 2017, when torrential rains caused a mudslide that killed at least eight people. Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Pence: Stopping ballistic attacks in Ukraine will ‘take the last fighting tool out of Vladimir Putin’s hands’
articles.summary: Former Vice President Mike Pence and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday stressed the importance of Ukraine having the capabilities to deter Russian ballistic missile strikes. During an interview on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” Pence said Russian forces have “shifted” to using high-arc ballistic missiles and cruise missiles to strike Ukraine. Those weapons require Patriot…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Mike Pence and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday stressed the importance of Ukraine having the capabilities to deter Russian ballistic missile strikes .

During an interview on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday,” Pence said Russian forces have “shifted” to using high-arc ballistic missiles and cruise missiles to strike Ukraine.

Those weapons require Patriot interceptors or terminal high-altitude area defense (THAAD) interceptors, the former vice president noted. Pence on Sunday addressed the National Prayer Breakfast in Ukraine and spoke with Zelensky.

“And President Zelensky again reiterated to me what he said publicly, that he’s anxious to see the United States make up to 5 percent of our Patriot resources available to make it possible for Ukraine to beat back those ballistic missile attacks,” Pence told host Chris Stirewalt.

“Stopping those ballistic missile attacks essentially will in many ways take the last fighting tool out of Vladimir Putin’s hands,” he said, referring to the Russian president.

While President Trump granted Ukraine a license to co-produce Patriot missiles in July, analysts have emphasized it will take years before the eastern European country is able to produce a suitable amount of those weapons.

Also complicating matters is the fact that the U.S. has exhausted nearly 80 percent of its THAAD interceptors and roughly half of its Patriots during the Iran war, CNN reported earlier this month .

Pence, though, denied Sunday that the Pentagon depleting its interceptor stockpiles is hurting Ukraine.

“I don’t see it that way, and I don’t think … the Ukrainians do either,” Pence told host Dana Bash on CNN’s “ State of the Union .”

July marked the deadliest month for civilians in Ukraine since May 2022, according to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.

Zelensky said Sunday he briefed Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and James Lankford (R-Okla.) in Kyiv on Russia’s “ongoing ballistic missile terror.”

The Ukrainian leader wrote on social media : “It is very important for Ukraine to have the capabilities to counter this, and implementing the decision to grant licenses for the production of Patriots could significantly help.”

Pence echoed Zelensky’s rhetoric, saying it is “essential” for the Trump administration and other foreign allies to continue backing Ukraine militarily.

Without further assistance, an “unprotected” Ukraine will be at risk of Russian attacks on energy infrastructure sites as the winter approaches, the former vice president stated.

“President Zelensky made it clear to me that Putin is going to use those ballistic missiles to strike, particularly not just like he did at a children’s hospital this week and not just as he did it at … a shopping mall this week,” Pence told Stirewalt. “But he’ll use that to take out the energy infrastructure here as winter approaches.”

articles.title: Donalds says he’s ‘working’ with Haitian leaders to stabilize government after end of TPS
articles.summary: Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), the GOP nominee for Florida governor, said Sunday he is “working” with leaders in Haiti to stabilize the country after the temporary protected status (TPS) of more than 300,000 Haitians migrants in the U.S. expired. “I’ve actually had meetings with the transitional government and the ambassador for the transitional government,” Donalds…
articles.body:
Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), the GOP nominee for Florida governor, said Sunday he is “working” with leaders in Haiti to stabilize the country after the temporary protected status (TPS) of more than 300,000 Haitians migrants in the U.S. expired.

“I’ve actually had meetings with the transitional government and the ambassador for the transitional government,” Donalds told host Margaret Brennan on CBS News’s “ Face the Nation .”

“They’re working on security forces right now as we speak to begin to stabilize Haiti, they’ve gotten about a quarter to half of the country under control from the gangs that basically took over Haiti,” added the Florida congressman, who won the Republican gubernatorial primary on Tuesday.

The Supreme Court earlier this summer allowed the Trump administration to revoke the TPS designation for Haitian migrants .

The high court ruled in a 6-3 decision, along ideological lines, that federal judges had no authority to weigh in on a challenge to the administration’s action brought by the migrants — reversing the February decision by U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes to pause the revocation .

Roughly 158,000 Haitian TPS holders lived in Florida as of January, according to a report from the immigration advocacy group Fwd.us .

Haitian TPS holders contribute $2.6 billion annually to the Sunshine State’s economy, with 93,000 Haitians in Florida working in industries such as agriculture, security and nursing, the report noted.

The Obama administration initially granted Haitians TPS in 2010 after an earthquake struck the Caribbean island. The State Department still warns Americans against traveling to Haiti over risks associated with crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest and limited healthcare.

But Donalds argued Sunday the TPS designation was not intended to last “into perpetuity with no end,” adding that creates the “wrong incentives to make sure that people can return to their home country, stabilize that country, and make sure that it returns to normalcy.”

articles.title: Vietnam: Gen Z seek justice for teen killed in ex-politician's car crash
articles.summary: Confirmation of the circumstances around Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's death have only spurred more questions.
articles.body:
Until recently, there would have been little to distinguish Vietnam's so-called Justice Tree from the hundreds of others lining the streets of Hanoi. Then the bouquets started piling up.

It was here that former politician Nguyen Sy Cuong was driving his BMW in May last year when he veered into the opposite lane and smashed into a motorbike carrying a father and his teenage daughter.

The father, Do Viet Hung, suffered a broken leg but survived. The daughter, 18-year-old Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy, died in hospital 10 days after the collision, which severed her right leg.

Fifteen months later, her death and the silence surrounding it has become a lightning rod for discontent among Vietnam's youth.

In early August, a legion of anonymous social media users started publishing millions of posts with the hashtags #NguyenSyCuong and #BMW across Facebook, Instagram, Threads and X. The users identified themselves as Gen Z – and they demanded accountability.

Initial discussions circled around whether the former politician was in fact the one who had caused the accident, and why authorities had only released sparse information.

Some pointed to reports that the driver of the BMW had the initials NSC and was born in 1961, leading to speculation that he was a former member of parliament. Others claimed the incident had been swept under the rug due to the influence of powerful figures.

Many reported that their posts had been deleted by social media platforms at the request of the Vietnamese government – providing screenshots of notifications as evidence. These claims could not be independently verified.

Expressions of outrage and calls for a proper investigation grew in number, volume and force.

Meanwhile, masked flower bearers started to appear, gravitating towards the scene of the incident and laying vibrant bouquets at the base of what has now been dubbed the Justice Tree. Police quickly arrived to get rid of the flowers, prompting mourners to create a virtual equivalent of the tree online - where hundreds of thousands of people have since sent tributes and paid respects.

Pressurised by more than a year's worth of growing suspicion and a rush of online attention, the issue had become too big to ignore.

Then, last Monday, the government made an extraordinary admission.

State broadcaster Vietnam Television (VTV) televised an official statement from authorities, confirming what had happened on the day of the incident. Former National Assembly deputy Nguyen Sy Cuong was indeed driving his car down Nguyen Huy Tu Street on 30 May, 2025, when his vehicle suddenly swerved across the road and into an oncoming motorcycle.

VTV cited police and prosecution sources who said that because Nguyen Sy Cuong "sincerely confessed and actively and fully remedied the consequences of his actions", Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's family had submitted a petition to exempt him from prosecution. The report did not specify what form this remedy took, but Nguyen Sy Cuong was cleared of all criminal liability.

While such a decision is lawful under Vietnam's legislation, lawyers have questioned whether the criminal proceedings were conducted in accordance with due process – or conducted at all. Social media users were quick to highlight his political connections and call for a more thorough investigation.

Such online pressure had yielded results in the past.

In March this year, a 66-year-old man driving under the influence of alcohol in Hanoi collided with seven other cars and three motorcycles in a chain-reaction crash that killed one woman and seriously injured two others.

In the wake of that incident, it emerged that the driver, Nguyen Van Sau, was a retired police colonel who had previously served as deputy director of a department under the Ministry of Public Security. Fearing that the driver was not being held culpable, the victim's family appealed for help. Social media users in turn amplified the issue, and after three months Nguyen Van Sau was charged with "violating regulations on participation in road traffic".

Who is To Lam, the ex-cop who wants to revamp Vietnam's success story?

British teen dies in reported Vietnam motorbike fall

Jailed Vietnamese tycoon's Birkin bags sell for more than $550K

Many now feel that a similar groundswell may be the only way to deliver justice for the teenager who died last year. But their efforts have been met with friction.

Do Viet Hung, the teenager's father, appeared in VTV's broadcast to thank internet users for their sympathy, but said the family was satisfied with the investigation's findings, and asked people to leave them alone. Notably, he also warned people "not to be drawn into the influence of reactionary elements".

Also appearing in the broadcast was a senior police official, who suggested that people were leveraging the incident to stoke dissent.

The Ministry of Public Security had "uncovered highly dangerous plots and intentions by hostile forces, reactionaries and bad actors to incite unrest and cause disorder", the official said.

"The ministry advises the public, especially young people, to remain fully alert and highly vigilant."

Similar rebukes have also started emerging on social media, with some claiming that conspiratorial forces were manipulating young people in Vietnam to stoke political discontent, manipulate public opinion online and rally people in real life ahead of the country's national holiday on 2 September.

Others have accused Gen Z Vietnamese of plotting a "colour revolution" – a term used to refer to mostly nonviolent protest movements that use specific colours or flowers as their symbol.

This is a familiar line of critique from Vietnamese authorities, who have previously labelled people's grievances or resentments as being untrue, unreasonable, or stemming from information fabricated by some "anti-government" or "reactionary" organisation.

Many in this case have said such accusations are baseless, insisting they are simply seeking justice for the victim of a fatal traffic accident. But the growing outrage has inevitably become a flashpoint amid broader, simmering grievances felt by Vietnam's youth.

Despite the Vietnamese government's tightening control over people's online freedom of expression – through measures ranging from intimidation and fines to criminal prosecution – public opinion in some corners has started to swerve against the Communist Party line.

On platforms such as Threads and Reddit, where anonymity is more normalised, many young people have expressed discontent towards various social issues: from the expansion of police power and land reclamation projects to exam cheating scandals and stricter regulation of online communication.

Such grievances echo those condemned by other Gen Z-led movements across the broader Asia region.

In countries like Bangladesh, India and Nepal, youth-led anti-government uprisings have over the past 12 months rallied immense support against the various pressure points of corruption, nepotism, economic inequality and democratic backsliding. Unofficially dubbed "the Asian Spring", the expanding influence of these movements has spread from Iran, Mongolia and the Maldives to the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

But protests in Vietnam have rarely, if ever, reached such fierce extremes. Vietnamese authorities have historically proven effective at detecting and stifling dissent before it boils over into action. Virtual places of mourning, anonymous social media posts, and online protests seem to be the most strident action many civilians here can afford to take.

Many are simply seeking justice for a teenager who was killed in a tragic accident, and accountability for a former lawmaker who appears to have been granted special clemency.

Yet even the mere suggestion that this incident could foment an uprising has provoked alarm – along with harsh reminders of the longstanding status quo in Vietnam's one-party state.

"Are these Gen Z kids planning a colour revolution using this accident?" reads one widely shared post. "Are they trying to emulate Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, and then create an Asian Spring? Remember, this is Vietnam! This is not Nepal, India, or Bangladesh!"

articles.title: The formidable challenges facing the next Tata Sons top boss
articles.summary: Corporate India's most coveted top job is open. But finding a new leader for Tata Sons is no easy task.
articles.body:
The shock resignation of Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran earlier this month has left corporate India's top job vacant. But finding his successor will be no easy task for the country's most revered conglomerate, whose sprawling $300bn empire spans Jaguar Land Rover and Air India as well as manufacturing iPhones for Apple.

Chandrasekaran resigned amid a deadlock over his reappointment and a widening rift with Tata Trusts - the charity arm which owns controlling shares of the unlisted commercial holding company.

The disagreements are said to have centred over a public listing of Tata Sons as well as capital allocation for the group's various new unlisted businesses, including semiconductors, e-commerce and aviation, all of which are bleeding money.

The group has been in the middle of the largest ever capital investment cycle, with tens of billions of dollars being deployed on everything from building India's first chip fabrication plant to manufacturing EV batteries and turning around Air India, which the Tatas bought from the government in 2022.

The new person at the helm will need to have an ability to assess and absorb the risks that have come with this breakneck expansion as well as rise up to numerous other challenges, Hetal Dalal from Institutional Investor Advisor Services (IiAS), a governance advisory firm, told the BBC.

"It is an incredibly difficult role not just for the individual who will get it but also for the selection committee to find someone. It requires a multitude of skillsets and experience from managing the Tata Trusts to the Tata Sons board, understanding various new businesses and being able to also have strong relationships with regulators and the government," Dalal said.

"There aren't many people running such large, diversified conglomerates. And will they leave their current roles to join the Tata Group?"

The complexity of the role has risen in recent years as the "collective losses of the new businesses are more than the cashflow generated by older companies like TCS, the group's software arm whose business model has been challenged by AI”, Nirmalya Kumar, who previously headed strategy at Tata Sons, told the BBC.

TCS has been the group's cash cow, contributing to some 85% of cash flows, but is no longer the pillar of support it once was.

According to Dalal, even though losses at privately held companies have mounted, the performance of publicly traded, CEO-run Tata companies has been strong.

The group has a good bench strength of internal candidates who could throw their hats in the ring. Yet, finding a candidate who's a straight "plug and play fit" will be difficult, she says.

"I think any person who comes in will have a set of skills and experience, but must be also groomed for the role."

Kumar, on the other hand, isn't convinced the internal names doing the rounds will fit the bill.

"The people internally are good executors of existing business models. Companies like Tata Steel and Tata Motors are almost running on auto-pilot with a CEO in charge. The new chairman will have to understand new business models of the four unlisted businesses that are losing money," he said.

For investors, the resignation is likely to usher in a period of prolonged uncertainty.

New leadership will bring a change in strategic direction at the group in terms of how a new chairman approaches the ambitious expansion Chandrasekharan undertook, say experts.

"Some of the bleeding businesses will need a strategic plan to be made profitable. [The new person] will need to decide whether to scale back or exit some investments," says Dalal.

Kumar says they will also need to communicate a clear plan to the market on how much further investment is needed and when a break-even is expected on these ambitious bets.

But most importantly, he adds, the focus will have to be on "driving alignment between the Trusts [the dominant shareholder] and Tata Sons".

The group's most successful run was under JRD Tata and Ratan Tata, when the relationship between the biggest shareholder and the operating company was frictionless as they were at the helm of both entities.

It broke down under Cyrus Mistry when there was a separation of the roles. Chandrasekharan's exit is the second instance where the chairman has resigned because of the rocky relationship with the Trusts.

The fact that the principal shareholder was not aligned on business strategy was perhaps a fundamental problem in the relationship breaking down, Mukund Rajan, former brand custodian at Tata Sons, told India Today news channel.

"You cannot have companies being run where the majority shareholder is either feeling ignored or not aligned with the way the company will be run going forward," Rajan said.

Repairing this relationship will have to be a key priority for whoever is next in the driving seat.

For now, the ongoing turmoil has dented the group's brand image, say experts.

Clear communication has been a major challenge with the Tatas, which does not bode well for the public markets, according to Dalal. While the holding company can argue that it is not publicly traded, what happens there has a direct impact on shareholders of the listed Tata universe, she adds.

"The priority should not be the volume of communication but about reducing uncertainty," Minari Shah, a communications advisor who previously worked with Tata Motors, told the BBC.

"That means demonstrating that governance mechanisms are working, reassuring stakeholders that business continuity is unaffected and providing clarity around the process for leadership transition. It is okay not to have all the answers immediately, as long as stakeholders have confidence that the disagreeing parties are in dialogue."

As of now, nearly two weeks after Chandrasekharan's resignation there have been no detailed public statements on either a succession roadmap, or the way ahead from either Tata Sons or Tata Trusts.

The former's annual general meeting also had to be adjourned because of a lack of quorum, leaving several governance and succession related decisions under a cloud at exactly the moment when shareholders of India's most iconic company will be looking for the greatest clarity.

articles.title: Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints as he visits Kyiv
articles.summary: It comes after Moscow warned of "consequences" over the reported use of British drones by Ukraine.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has promised to keep up the pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats", on his first official visit to Ukraine as UK prime minister.

Burnham met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and chaired his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

He said the coalition was "doing everything we can" while urging the US Congress to "ratchet up" economic pressure on Russia.

The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the long-range weapon domestically.

UK missiles offer may help Ukraine - but they are not what Zelensky needs most Published 1 day ago

UK missiles offer may help Ukraine - but they are not what Zelensky needs most

Briton fighting for Russia killed in Ukraine Published 1 day ago

Briton fighting for Russia killed in Ukraine

Burnham said allies were doing "everything we can" to "dig into our own stocks and help others dig into their stocks" of air defences to protect Ukraine.

"This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia, the moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war," Burnham said, praising the "strength" of the Ukrainian people.

"Ukraine has been Europe's protector, not a drain on our security but the front line in keeping Europe safe."

It comes after Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov criticised the UK's decision to share the missile blueprints. Peskov said it prevented "even the slightest progress" towards achieving peace.

He told reporters on Monday that the Russian military was already gathering data to locate any missile production sites to destroy them.

"Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire," he added.

In response, Burnham said: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?"

He said the issue of missile interceptors would be the main topic at the coalition of the willing meeting.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, former Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Fedorov said the UK could face a "semi-military" response in retaliation for sharing military blueprints with Ukraine, but specified this would be "not by Russia, but from unknown sources".

"Something might happen with enterprises, with factories which are producing drones for Ukraine," Fedorov said.

Asked if he was OK with a potential attack, he said: "No, I don't think it's okay, because the problem is that we are now facing, in front of the danger, that Ukrainian conflict will be beyond Ukrainian borders."

Burnham has been reaffirming the UK's backing for Kyiv in the wake of escalating Russian strikes on Ukraine in recent weeks - including one on a shopping centre on Friday that killed at least 16 people.

In a joint statement after the meeting, Burnham and co-chairs French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the group would aim to strength Kyiv's air defences "as a matter or urgent priority".

They also condemned Moscow's "systemic and escalating strikes against Ukraine's cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and pledged to "constrain Russia's war chest through sanctions and actions against the "shadow fleet".

The Coalition of the Willing is a partnership of 34 countries including Ukraine. Members met on Monday in either Kyiv or by video conference, with a release stating "leaders once again reaffirmed their commitment to support Ukraine's independence".

It came as the European Union said it had released €6.1bn (£5.2bn) in military aid for Ukraine to boost its air defences. The finance is part of a wider €90bn loan from the EU to Ukraine.

The UK and Ukraine have also announced a new military technology partnership , external giving British experts access to Kyiv's Avengers AI Labs database.

Downing Street says Ukraine has used sensors and cameras to capture data across the battlefield and it can be used to train AI models "to solve key national security challenges" faced by both countries.

On Monday morning the prime minister laid flowers at the graves of Ukrainian soldiers during a service at the National Military Memorial Cemetery.

He accepted an award from Zelensky on behalf of the British people recognising the UK's support for Ukraine during an independence day event outside the St Sofia cathedral in Kyiv.

In a speech, Burnham compared Ukraine's resistance to Russia to the UK's fight with Nazi Germany, saying: "My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st."

In a statement issued ahead of the visit, the prime minister said: "On Ukraine's 35th anniversary of independence, the Ukrainian people should be in no doubt: the UK is behind you today and for as long as it takes.

"I am proud of the contribution our country has made to Ukraine and I want the Ukrainian people to hear it directly from me that our support will not waver. After all, Ukraine's security is our security."

He said the friendship Ukraine shared with the UK would "long outlast Russia's illegal war", adding: "Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."

Moscow earlier warned of "consequences" over the use of British drones by Ukraine in its recent ramping up of strikes on Russian infrastructure.

Kyiv has stepped up long-range attacks on Moscow and other Russian regions, targeting oil refineries and warehouses of the country's largest online retailer, Wildberries.

The government is allowing UK defence company MBDA to declassify information on its components for the Scalp missile, as Ukraine and France aim to establish assembly lines in Ukraine.

Scalp missiles and its UK-produced version, the Storm Shadow, have already been provided to Kyiv by both Britain and France and used to hit military targets inside Russia.

What are the Storm Shadow missiles Ukraine has fired into Russia?

Ukraine hopes it can also be given more Patriot interceptor missiles, with Zelensky again asking for more of the weapon, which are used to combat Russia's ballistic missiles.

Ukraine has been relying on American supplies of the Patriots, but its stockpiles are running low due to the war in Iran, leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian attacks.

The Russian embassy in the UK has accused Britain of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis", saying "the deeper its involvement in the conflict... the higher the price it will pay".

In response, Burnham said last week: "We are not fair-weather friends, we will be there in Ukraine's hour of need and that won't change."

Asked on Tuesday about the Russian threat, Burnham maintained the UK was "providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself and that's been the British position all the way through this conflict, by previous prime ministers - it remains the case with me".

The visit comes as Russia confirmed its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, had left his post in London in recent weeks.

The Kremlin is yet to put forward a replacement but Russia's embassy to the UK told the BBC it did not reflect an intention to downgrade diplomatic relations between the two nations.

Deadly exchanges between Russia and Ukraine continued overnight, with two children killed and seven injured when Ukrainian drone debris hit a private children's centre in Russia, local authorities say.

A warehouse belonging to online retailer Ozon was also set on fire, two days after Ukraine said it would target the company for selling dual use items that could be used by the military.

It was at the third night in the row that Ozon's warehouses had been targeted, with the company confirming on Saturday that a logistics centre in the Samara region had been hit and a warehouse in Orenburg on Sunday.

Three people were also killed in a Russian attack on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.

articles.title: 'I didn't speak the Queen's English': Why people worry about their accents
articles.summary: A survey on attitudes towards accents suggests that so-called "accent bias" is still an issue in many workplaces.
articles.body:
Growing up in Manchester, Mia Tanswell didn't give her accent much thought - until her first week at university in Loughborough.

"I knew people were going to notice that I was northern and that I didn't speak the 'Queen's English'," the 22-year-old says.

"Definitely in seminars I would sometimes feel like my accent would sound a bit less intellectual than other people, especially if I was the only northern student in the classroom."

She's not alone. Fresh polling seen by the BBC suggests many workers still see so-called "accent bias" as a problem.

The survey found one in 10 people in Britain feel anxious or self-conscious about their accent in high stakes professional settings such as speaking up in a business meeting.

The research, conducted by the organisation More in Common of more than 3,300 adults across England, Scotland and Wales, found accent-related anxiety in work settings like these was highest among Geordies - from the region around Newcastle - and those with an east London - or Cockney - accent (at 19%), followed by people with a Welsh accent (at 18%).

Around 5% of respondents believed their accent had cost them a promotion, pay rise or senior role. "Brummies" - people from Birmingham - were the most likely to feel this, at 13%.

Respondents with a West Country accent reported the highest rate of having their accent mocked or criticised by colleagues, at 15%, followed by 13% of those with a Geordie accent.

The poll was commissioned by Common Ground, an organisation which aims to promote social cohesion. Its founder, Lara Newman, has worked in construction, property and the built environment industry for more than 30 years, and says she changed her own accent to get ahead in the workplace.

"I am incredibly realistic about what would have happened had I gone to university or gone into the workplace with a strong west country accent," she says. "I felt like that was going to be an issue for me."

Common Ground aims to support people from disadvantaged backgrounds into work but she says one of the layers creating a barrier to them is accent.

"I think there is a problem in the sense that [an accent] implies a level of education or otherwise. It implies class," she says.

Martha Powell, 24, from Newport in south Wales is proud of her accent.

"I love my accent, if anything I wish it was more Welsh," she says.

But she still fears people "make assumptions" based on her accent so at networking events she gravitates towards others with a Welsh accent.

"I wish I would be able to stand out a little bit more, but I think I adapt my accent depending on where I am in the country."

Softening an accent is common, the survey results suggest, with 13% of Britons polled admitting to changing the way they speak to sound more professional, with Cockneys and Scots more likely to do this.

A foreign, rather than a regional accent, can also be a barrier. When Benjaimin Aidomoan came to the UK four years ago from the Czech Republic aged 16, he didn't speak a word of English.

He picked up the language, but four years on says his accent has made job-hunting more difficult.

"You can just see on many people's faces, that the expression and the way they are looking at you and the way they are talking to you kind of changes," he says.

Benjaimin, who now works in a restaurant, believes most employers do look beyond accents.

"It's about who you are, how you present yourself, what is your attitude and how hard you're willing to work," he says.

Most employers would say that is at least their ambition, to treat applicants and employees equally, regardless of their accent.

Charlotte Davies, career expert at LinkedIn, says while there is still progress to be made "the direction of travel is encouraging".

"Hiring is increasingly about skills, not background or polish.

"Your accent is part of your story, and the workplaces getting this right, treat that as a strength, not something to smooth out," she says.

Sian Jackson, a partner at law firm Mills & Reeve, says her company has recently changed its approach to encourage more local hiring and a diversity of accents.

"We don't judge, we scrutinise based on capability beyond somebody's accent, or appearance. Like any other prejudice or bias it's about being conscious of it so you can then set it aside," she says.

"We feel we've come a long way as a firm, but we are behind nationally compared to things like gender, so there is more progress to be made on accents."

articles.title: Trump diz que Irã está 'completamente colapsado' | G1
articles.standfirst: Declaração ocorre no dia em que os EUA prometeram divulgar novas sanções ao Irã. Presidente dos EUA disse que a ofensiva será a "operação econômica mais esmagadora" contra um país.
articles.summary: O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta segunda-feira (24) que o Irã está "colapsando completamente".
articles.body:
O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, em 10 de agosto de 2026. — Foto: Kylie Cooper/Reuters

O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta segunda-feira (24) que o Irã está "colapsando completamente".

A afirmação ocorre no dia em que os Estados Unidos devem publicar novas sanções ao regime iraniano, dentro do que chamou de "o dia D" de uma guerra econômica que anunciou contra Teerã . Trump disse que a ofensiva será a "operação econômica mais esmagadora" contra um país.

"O Irã está colapsando completamente", escreveu Trump em sua rede social Truth Social.

Parte da "guerra econômica" de Trump será tentar costurar acordos com países do Oriente Médio e também ameaçá-los com sanções caso sigam negociando com o Irã, para isolar Teerã.

No sábado (22), o presidente do Parlamento do Irã, Mohammad Ghalibaf, também o principal negociador do país com os EUA, disse que o governo iraniano recebeu mensagens de vizinhos citando a criação de "novos acordos de segurança e cooperação econômica" .

Nesta segunda, o regime dos aiatolás retrucou. O Ministério das Relações Exteriores do Irã afirmou que os países vizinhos que optarem por aderir à campanha de pressão econômica dos Estados Unidos contra o país poderão enfrentar "consequências".

O Ministério dos Transportes atualizou, nesta segunda-feira (24), o aplicativo CNH do Brasil. Com a mudança, os motoristas poderão consultar pela plataforma as passagens registradas em pedágios do sistema "free flow".

🔎 O free flow é um sistema de pedágio eletrônico sem cancelas que permite cobrar a tarifa sem que o motorista precise parar ou reduzir a velocidade.

✅ Clique aqui para seguir o canal do g1 Carros no WhatsApp

Segundo o Ministério dos Transportes, todas as passagens por rodovias estarão listadas no aplicativo, “sejam elas federais ou estaduais. Além da consulta, o cidadão terá acesso a informações centralizadas para identificar, pela plataforma, a concessionária responsável e acessar o respectivo canal indicado para pagamento do pedágio”.

O ministro dos Transportes, George Santoro, afirmou que apenas uma das concessionárias que operam o sistema free flow no Brasil ainda não está integrada à plataforma: a responsável pelo Rodoanel, em São Paulo.

Segundo o ministro, enquanto a concessionária não estiver integrada à plataforma, não poderão ser aplicadas multas pelo não pagamento da tarifa no sistema free flow, e a homologação para o uso da tecnologia será revogada.

Para consultar as passagens pelo free flow, o motorista precisa:

Escolher e tocar no veículo na lista exibida ;

Nessa área, o motorista pode consultar as passagens registradas no sistema free flow, acessar o canal de pagamento da concessionária e acompanhar a confirmação do pagamento.

As passagens ficam registradas no aplicativo por até cinco anos. O motorista tem até 30 dias após o recebimento da notificação sobre a passagem pelo pórtico para pagar a tarifa.

“Nada é mais crítico para a concessionária do que a receita. Agora, todos nós que trafegarmos pelo pórtico do free flow recebemos, pelo menos, dois avisos: um para a passagem e o segundo quando estiver acabando o prazo de 30 dias para o pagamento”, disse Marco Aurélio Barcelos, diretor-presidente da Associação Brasileira de Concessionárias de Rodovias (ABCR).

As notificações, o registro da passagem e o valor do pedágio eletrônico ficam disponíveis apenas para o proprietário do veículo . Diferentemente de uma multa de trânsito, a cobrança da tarifa não pode ser transferida para outro motorista.

O ministro George Santoro disse ao g1 que o Ministério dos Transportes espera facilitar o pagamento das tarifas com a nova ferramenta. Segundo ele, caso a medida não traga os resultados esperados, o governo poderá permitir que o pagamento seja feito diretamente pelo aplicativo.

“A gente não quis impor uma solução de pagamento, deixando o mercado tentar encontrar uma solução própria. Se o mercado em pouco tempo não der uma solução, nós vamos dar uma solução. Junto do Serpro, nós vamos criar um portal de pagamento com algum parceiro, ou algum integrador", disse o ministro.

O usuário também pode contestar pelo aplicativo uma passagem que, segundo ele, não tenha sido realizada pelo veículo.

Para motoristas que utilizam tags, nada muda: a cobrança continua sendo feita automaticamente pela plataforma contratada, com o pagamento direcionado à empresa responsável pelo serviço.

Confusão fez ministério suspender multas

Antes da nova funcionalidade, o motorista precisava procurar o canal de atendimento de cada concessionária para consultar e pagar as tarifas. A falta de um sistema centralizado dificultava os pagamentos e abria espaço para golpes com sites falsos.

Desde abril deste ano, o Ministério dos Transportes suspendeu 3,7 milhões de multas relacionadas ao não pagamento de pedágios eletrônicos . A medida também suspendeu os pontos na CNH decorrentes dessas infrações.

Segundo a pasta, a suspensão abriu prazo para os ajustes necessários e para a integração da comunicação das concessionárias com o sistema do governo federal.

Para aplicar a multa, o governo federal recebe da concessionária a informação sobre a falta de pagamento e registra a infração no aplicativo CNH do Brasil. A evasão de pedágio, seja em praças tradicionais ou no free flow, gera multa de R$ 195,23 e cinco pontos na CNH.

"Está em elaboração uma deliberação do Conselho Nacional de Trânsito (Contran) para prorrogar o prazo de homologação até dezembro de 2026. A proposta ainda está em tramitação interna e aguarda manifestação da Consultoria Jurídica", disse a pasta em nota.

Com a prorrogação, o motorista que passou pelo pórtico do free flow e não pagou a tarifa terá uma nova oportunidade para quitar a dívida sem multa. Não se trata, porém, de perdão: a penalidade poderá ser aplicada se o pagamento não for feito dentro do novo prazo.

O que é o pedágio eletrônico (free flow)?

O pedágio eletrônico, ou free flow (“fluxo livre”, em inglês), é um sistema de cobrança sem cabines ou cancelas e que não exige o uso de tag pelo motorista.

Nesse sistema, câmeras e sensores identificam o veículo sem que o motorista precise parar ou reduzir a velocidade. Em algumas rodovias, a tecnologia também permite cobrar de acordo com o trecho percorrido.

O pedágio eletrônico já é adotado em mais de 20 países, como Noruega, Portugal, Estados Unidos, Itália, China e Chile — um dos pioneiros na América Latina na implementação do sistema.

Pórtico free flow — Foto: divulgação/Concessionária Novo Litoral

Não. O sistema free flow identifica o veículo para fazer a cobrança da tarifa. A multa não é aplicada pela simples passagem pelo pórtico, mas pelo não pagamento do pedágio dentro do prazo.

O não pagamento configura evasão de pedágio, uma infração grave, com multa de R$ 195,23 e cinco pontos na CNH.

O free flow combina a tecnologia das tags já utilizadas no Brasil com câmeras e sensores capazes de identificar veículos que não possuem o dispositivo.

Diversas câmeras e sensores são instalados nos pórticos fixos nas rodovias. Eles identificam os veículos com tag ou fazem a leitura das placas para determinar quem será cobrado.

Algumas câmeras capturam imagens em 3D para identificar o tipo de veículo, o número de eixos e quais deles estão suspensos. Essas informações permitem calcular corretamente a tarifa, especialmente no caso de caminhões.

Luzes infravermelhas são utilizadas para garantir a identificação dos veículos mesmo em condições adversas, como neblina ou fumaça.

articles.title: Piloto brasileiro desenha 'Lito' no céu dos EUA em homenagem | G1
articles.standfirst: Voo de três horas formou o nome do influenciador no céu do Texas. Lito foi diagnosticado com uma doença neurológica rara e busca acesso a tratamento experimental.
articles.summary: Voo de três horas formou o nome do influenciador no céu do Texas. Lito foi diagnosticado com uma doença neurológica rara e busca acesso a tratamento experimental.
articles.body:
Piloto escreveu o nome de Lito durante um voo no Texas, nos Estados Unidos — Foto: FlightRadar24.com/Reprodução

Um piloto brasileiro usou um avião para fazer uma homenagem ao influenciador e ex-mecânico de aviação Lito Sousa nos céus dos Estados Unidos , nesta segunda-feira (24). A homenagem foi feita após Lito ser diagnosticado com a doença de Creutzfeldt-Jakob (DCJ).

✅ Siga o canal de notícias internacionais do g1 no WhatsApp

O caso de Lito tem causado mobilização nas redes sociais . Por ser uma doença neurológica rara, grave e de rápida progressão, seguidores e o próprio influenciador pedem que ele tenha acesso a um tratamento experimental. Veja mais abaixo.

Na noite desta segunda-feira, o piloto Enderson Rafael fez uma homenagem a Lito. A bordo de um Cessna 150M, ele desenhou o nome do influenciador no céu de uma região próxima à cidade de Dallas, no Texas.

Dados do site FlightRadar24 mostram que o voo durou pouco mais de três horas. Na plataforma, o trajeto chegou a figurar entre os mais monitorados do mundo.

No Instagram, Rafael publicou fotos da homenagem. Em uma das postagens, afirmou que levou três horas para escrever o nome de Lito no céu, formando um desenho maior do que a cidade de São Paulo.

Lito fez a primeira aparição pública após o diagnóstico no domingo (23). Em um vídeo publicado no Instagram, o influenciador pediu para ser submetido a um tratamento experimental desenvolvido por pesquisadores da Universidade Harvard.

Antes da publicação do vídeo, seguidores de Lito já haviam iniciado uma mobilização nas redes sociais para tentar incluí-lo em um estudo experimental com o medicamento ION717, da farmacêutica Ionis Pharmaceuticals.

Segundo o relato publicado no Instagram, dois estudos são considerados promissores pela família. No momento, porém, nenhum dos dois está recebendo novos participantes.

De acordo com o relato, um dos estudos é ligado à Universidade Harvard, nos Estados Unidos. O outro é multicêntrico e envolve centros de pesquisa em Paris, na França, além de Alemanha e Inglaterra.

Mila Seidl, esposa do influenciador, disse que está animada com a corrente de ajuda que o marido vem recebendo de organizações médicas e amigos de Lito ao redor do mundo.

Ela afirma que já entrou em contato com os responsáveis pelos dois estudos e busca uma forma de incluir Lito, mesmo que seja necessário avaliar uma possível exceção aos critérios de participação.

“Eu tenho 0% de chance, mas se eu tiver 1% de chance em qualquer lugar, a gente quer esse 1%”, afirmou Mila em um vídeo.

Lito Sousa é dono do canal 'Aviões e Músicas', no YouTube, onde explica, em linguagem acessível, como funcionam aviões, procedimentos de segurança, turbulências e acidentes aéreos. — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

O diagnóstico da doença de Creutzfeldt-Jakob exige uma investigação cuidadosa para descartar outras condições que podem provocar sintomas semelhantes.

Em geral, a doença começa com alterações rapidamente progressivas na cognição , afetando a memória, a autonomia e a capacidade de realizar atividades cotidianas. As alterações motoras costumam aparecer posteriormente.

“A gente está falando de uma doença rara, e ainda de uma manifestação inicial com sintomas motores, e não cognitivos, mantendo a lucidez”, explica o neurologista Felipe Schmidt, coordenador do Serviço de Neuroimunologia do HUPE/Uerj.

Após a confirmação do diagnóstico, o tratamento é voltado principalmente para o controle dos sintomas e o conforto do paciente. Atualmente, não há uma terapia específica capaz de curar a doença de Creutzfeldt-Jakob ou interromper sua progressão.

“É basicamente suporte e conforto. Então, tratar a dor, tratar os movimentos involuntários, em especial a mioclonia, enfim, tentar dar mais conforto para aquele paciente e aquela família”, afirma o neurologista.
